subject: MATH
overview: Teach each lesson in about 60 minutes: 10 minutes of counting or fact warm-up, 30 minutes of hands-on work with real objects (counters, cubes, ten-frames, blocks), and 15–20 minutes of practice and talk. Always let your child build or draw a problem before writing the equation, and ask 'How do you know?' every day so explanations become a habit. Keep the equal sign meaning 'the same as', and revisit facts within 10 with short games all year until they are automatic.

weeks.prep: Gather 3–4 zip bags of 8–20 beans or buttons, two ten-frame mats (draw a 2×5 grid on paper), a 0–20 number line, sticky notes, and dot/ten-frame cards (draw 0–10 dots on index cards).
misconceptions: Counting the same object twice or skipping one: have your child move each bean onto a ten-frame square as they say each number (one touch, one word).
Writing numerals backward (e.g., Ɛ for 3): use the 'start at the top' rule and trace a model with a finger before writing.

Counting on by starting with the first number ('7, 8, 9' for 7 + 3 = 9 gives only 9 if you count 7 as a jump): teach that you say the start number, then count 3 more jumps: 'seven... eight, nine, ten.'

days.guide: Hand your child a bag of beans and say, 'Let's find out how many.' Model placing one bean in each ten-frame box, filling the top row left to right, then the bottom row. When a frame is full, say 'That's ten,' then count on from ten for the extras and write the numeral on a sticky note.

questions.q: A full ten-frame and 4 more beans. How many beans?
questions.a: 14 — ten in the full frame, then 11, 12, 13, 14.

questions.q: Count 17 beans onto ten-frames. How many frames are full?
questions.a: 1 full frame (10) with 7 beans in the second frame.

days.guide: Show each numeral 0–20 on a model strip. Say the rule: 'Every number starts at the top.' Have your child trace 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9 with a finger in the air, then on paper three times each, then write 0–20 in order while you watch for reversals.

questions.q: Write 13 and 15. Which way do the 3 and 5 face?
questions.a: Both open to the left side (bumps/belly face right); 13 is a 1 then a 3, 15 is a 1 then a 5.

questions.q: Where do you start writing a 5?
questions.a: At the top: draw the short line down, the belly around, then the flag across the top.

days.guide: Put a finger on 7 on the number line and say 'seven,' then hop 3 times saying 'eight, nine, ten.' Explain you land on the answer. Play 'Start at ___, count on ___' with your child choosing start numbers under 17 and counting on 1, 2, or 3.

questions.q: Start at 7, count on 3. Where do you land?
Start at 12, count on 2.
Start at 16, count on 4.

days.guide: Flash a dot or ten-frame card for 3 seconds, then hide it. Ask 'How many? How did you see it?' Praise seeing groups ('I saw 5 on top and 2 more') rather than counting by ones.

questions.q: A ten-frame shows a full top row and 3 dots on the bottom. How many?
A ten-frame has all boxes full except 1. How many dots?

days.guide: Run the check as a short, friendly interview. Have your child count 3 collections aloud while you watch for one-to-one matching, then dictate numerals (e.g., 6, 12, 19, 0, 15, 20) and give 5 count-on starts.

questions.q: Start at 5, count on 3.
Write the number nineteen.

weeks.assessment_key: Counting interview: Proficient = counts each collection (e.g., 9, 14, 20) with one touch per object, says the last number as 'how many', and organizes on ten-frames. Count-on: 5+3→8, 9+2→11, 11+3→14, 14+4→18, 17+3→20. Dictation answers: whatever numbers you say written correctly with no reversals (e.g., 6, 12, 19, 0, 15, 20). 4 = all correct; 3 = one error or reversal; 2 = counts but loses track over 15 or several reversals; 1 = cannot count past 10 reliably — reteach with ten-frames.

weeks.prep: Counters (two colors, or beans painted on one side), a cup, drawing paper, and 6 short story problems written on cards (see the key).
misconceptions: Writing only the answer (7) instead of the whole equation: model saying the story as an equation ('4 red and 3 green is 7') then write 4 + 3 = 7.
Counting all from 1 every time: once the child knows one group, cover it and say 'You know there are 6 here — count on from 6.'
Thinking the + sign means 'and then count again from 1': connect + to 'joined with' using two piles pushed together.

days.guide: Tell the story 'I have 4 red apples and 3 green apples' while your child lays out 4 red and 3 green counters. Push the groups together and count, then show how to write 4 + 3 = 7 and read it aloud. Repeat with 2 more put-together stories.

questions.q: 2 dogs and 5 cats are in the yard. How many animals?
3 blue cars and 3 red cars. How many cars?

days.guide: Tell 'add to' stories where more join: '5 birds sit on a fence. 2 more fly in.' Have your child draw 5 birds, then 2, circle all, and write 5 + 2 = 7. Ask what number the story starts with and what number joins.

questions.q: 5 birds, 2 more come. How many now?
6 kids are playing. 3 more join. How many now?

days.guide: Show 6 + 2 with counters: cover the 6 with your hand and say 'six... seven, eight' while touching the 2. Teach your child to start with the bigger number even if it comes second (2 + 6: start at 6).

questions.q: 2 + 7 = ? Which number do you start from?
questions.a: 9; start from 7, the bigger number, and count on 2.

days.guide: Shake 6 two-color counters in a cup and spill. Your child records the red + yellow combination (e.g., 4 + 2 = 6). Repeat about 10 times and then list all the ways for 6 found.

questions.q: List all the ways to make 6 with two colors.
If 1 counter landed red, how many landed yellow?

days.guide: Read each of 6 story problems aloud (your child should not have to read). Let your child draw or use counters, then write an equation for each.

questions.q: Mom bought 3 pears and 4 bananas. How many pieces of fruit?
5 ants were on a log. 4 more came. How many now?

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested 6 problems and answers: 1) 2 cats and 4 dogs: 2 + 4 = 6. 2) 5 frogs, 3 more hop in: 5 + 3 = 8. 3) 1 red ball and 6 blue balls: 1 + 6 = 7. 4) 4 cookies, Dad gives 4 more: 4 + 4 = 8. 5) 7 fish, 2 more swim in: 7 + 2 = 9. 6) 3 apples and 7 apples: 3 + 7 = 10. Score: 1 point for the correct answer and 1 for a matching equation (12 points). 10–12 proficient; 7–9 developing; below 7 reteach with counters.

weeks.prep: Counters, 3–4 paper cups, a 0–20 number line, drawing paper, and a few cookies or crackers for acting out 'take from' stories.
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller number from the bigger no matter the story, or writing 3 − 8: remind that we start with the whole amount (8) and take away part.
Counting back incorrectly by saying the starting number as the first jump (for 8 − 2, saying '8, 7' and answering 7): model hopping off the start: 'eight... seven, six.'
Thinking 'take apart' (9 kids, 4 girls) is addition because there are no 'taken away' words: draw 9, circle the 4 girls, and show the rest are the boys.

days.guide: Put 8 cookies (or counters) out and act out eating 3. Ask how many are left and count. Write 8 − 3 = 5 and read it 'eight take away three equals five.' Do 3 more take-from stories.

questions.q: 8 cookies, eat 3. How many left?
7 balloons, 2 fly away. How many left?

days.guide: Show 7 counters, then hide some under a cup while your child closes their eyes. They count the counters still showing and figure out how many are hidden. Write the subtraction (7 − 4 = 3 when 4 are showing).

questions.q: 7 counters total, 4 showing. How many are hidden?
7 total, 6 showing. How many hidden?

days.guide: On the number line, start at the first number and hop backward, saying the numbers you land on. Practice − 1, − 2, and − 3 from numbers up to 15.

questions.q: 9 − 2 = ? (count back)

days.guide: Read 'There are 9 kids. 4 are girls. How many are boys?' Have your child draw 9 stick people, circle the 4 girls, and count the rest. Write 9 − 4 = 5 and also 4 + 5 = 9.

questions.q: 9 kids, 4 are girls. How many boys?
10 pets: 6 are dogs, the rest are cats. How many cats?

days.guide: Give a mix of add and subtract story problems. Before solving each, ask 'Is the amount getting bigger or smaller?' Have your child explain one strategy out loud (drawing, counting on, counting back).

questions.q: 6 frogs, 3 hop away. How many left?
4 crayons, 4 more. How many?

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested problems: 1) 9 apples, 3 eaten: 9 − 3 = 6. 2) 5 birds + 4 birds: 5 + 4 = 9. 3) 10 bubbles, 7 pop: 10 − 7 = 3. 4) 8 kids, 5 are boys, how many girls: 8 − 5 = 3. 5) 2 + 6 = 8 marbles. 6) 7 cars, 1 drives away: 6. Verbal explanation rubric: 4 = names strategy and shows it ('I started at 9 and counted back 3: 8, 7, 6'); 3 = correct strategy with some prompting; 2 = correct answer but cannot explain; 1 = chooses wrong operation.

weeks.prep: Connecting cubes (or LEGO bricks), a deck of cards with face cards removed (Ace = 1, add paper 0 cards), dot cards, a number path 0–20 with some blanks, and a printed Unit 1 test (see key).
misconceptions: Answering 'how many more' with the bigger total (9 instead of 3): line up the towers side by side and point only to the extra cubes that stick up.
Thinking 'fewer' means 'more': practice with physical towers — the shorter tower has fewer.
Losing track when counting backward across the teens: practice saying 20 down to 10 with a number path in view.

days.guide: Build a tower of 9 and a tower of 6 and stand them side by side. Ask which has more and how you know, then point to the cubes that are 'extra' on the taller tower and count them: 3 more.

questions.q: Towers of 9 and 6: how many more is 9?
Towers of 5 and 8: which has fewer, and by how many?

days.guide: Read 'Ana has 7 stickers, Ben has 4. How many more does Ana have?' Build a 7-tower and a 4-tower, match cube to cube, and count the unmatched cubes. Write 7 − 4 = 3 or 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.q: Ana 7, Ben 4. How many more does Ana have?
Jo has 10 marbles and Kim has 6. How many fewer does Kim have?

days.guide: Play 'War' with cards 0–10: each flips a card, the bigger card wins, and the winner must say how many more (e.g., '8 is 3 more than 5'). Use cubes to check when unsure.

questions.q: You flip 8, I flip 5. Who has more and by how much?
You flip 2, I flip 9. By how much does 9 win?

days.guide: Count together from 1 to 20, then 20 back to 0 while pointing to the number path. Then have your child fill in blanks on a number path such as 11, __, 13, __, __, 16.

questions.q: What number comes just before 15? Just after 19?

days.guide: Give the Unit 1 test one section at a time, reading every problem aloud. Allow counters or drawings.

questions.q: Count back from 13 to 8.
Sam has 8 grapes, Tia has 5. How many more does Sam have?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (suggested) with answers: 1) Count 16 objects → 16. 2) Write numerals dictated: 7, 11, 14, 18, 20. 3) Start at 9, count on 3 → 12. 4) 3 + 4 = 7. 5) 5 + 3 story → 8. 6) 9 − 2 = 7. 7) 8 cookies, 5 eaten → 3. 8) 6 kids, 2 are girls, boys? → 4. 9) Towers 7 and 3: how many more? → 4. 10) Fill 16, 15, __, 13 → 14. Score 9–10 proficient; 7–8 developing; under 7 reteach weak items.

weeks.prep: Ten-frame, two-color counters, a deck of playing cards (remove face cards and 10s; Ace = 1), number-bond sheet (circle with two smaller circles), and a 1-minute make-10 list for Friday.
misconceptions: Thinking 5 + 5 is the only way to make 10: fill a ten-frame with two colors in every way and list them.
Forgetting 0 + 10 and 10 + 0: show a ten-frame that is all one color.
Mixing up the whole and the parts in a number bond: the whole always goes in the top (big) circle.

days.guide: Have your child fill a ten-frame with red counters then swap one at a time to yellow, recording each: 9 + 1, 8 + 2, ... 1 + 9. Ask what pattern they notice (one number goes down by 1 while the other goes up by 1).

questions.q: 7 red on the ten-frame. How many yellow to fill it?
What goes with 4 to make 10?

days.guide: Deal 5 cards each. On your turn, ask for the card that makes 10 with one in your hand ('I have 3; do you have a 7?'). Lay down pairs that make 10 and say the fact.

questions.q: You hold a 2. What card do you ask for?
You hold a 5. What do you ask for?

days.guide: Put out 7 counters and have your child split them into two groups every way possible, drawing a number bond for each (7 on top; 2 and 5 below). Repeat with 8.

questions.q: Name all the ways to split 7 into two parts.
questions.a: 0 and 7, 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4 (and turned around).

questions.q: 8 is 3 and what?

days.guide: Write 6 + ? = 10. Put 6 counters on the ten-frame and count the empty boxes (4). For ? + 3 = 8, put 3 counters out, count up to 8, and find the missing part.
Give a 1-minute make-10 list (e.g., 7 + __ = 10) and then the number-bond sheet. Celebrate improvement, not speed alone.

questions.q: Number bond: whole 9, one part 4. Other part?

weeks.assessment_key: Make-10 list answers: 9+1, 8+2, 7+3, 6+4, 5+5, 4+6, 3+7, 2+8, 1+9, 0+10 (so blanks are: for 9→1, 8→2, 7→3, 6→4, 5→5, 4→6, 3→7, 2→8, 1→9, 0→10). Number bonds (suggested): whole 7 parts 3 & 4; whole 8 parts 2 & 6; whole 6 parts 1 & 5; whole 9 parts 4 & 5; whole 10 parts 7 & 3. Proficient = 8+ of 10 make-10 facts in 1 minute and all bonds correct.

weeks.prep: A small mirror, counters, dominoes, 2 dice, an egg carton, and pictures/toys showing doubles (spider = 8 legs, 2 hands = 10 fingers).
misconceptions: Thinking a double means 'twice the first number plus something' or confusing 4 + 4 with 4 + 5: use the mirror to show two equal groups.
For near doubles, adding 1 to the wrong number or forgetting the +1: say 'double the smaller, then one more.'
Believing 2 + 7 and 7 + 2 have different answers: build both cube trains and turn one around to see they match.

days.guide: Place 3 counters next to a mirror so your child sees 6. Say '3 + 3 = 6.' Repeat with 1–5, writing each doubles fact in a list.

questions.q: What double makes 6?

days.guide: Hunt for doubles at home: an egg carton (6 + 6 = 12), spider legs (4 + 4 = 8), hands (5 + 5 = 10). Your child draws two and writes the fact under each drawing.

questions.q: A spider has 4 legs on each side. How many legs?
An egg carton has 6 in each row. How many eggs?

days.guide: Show a domino with 4 and 5. Say 'I know 4 + 4 = 8, and 5 is one more than 4, so 4 + 5 = 9.' Have your child sort dominoes into doubles and doubles-plus-one and solve them.

questions.q: 4 + 5 = ? Explain.

days.guide: Build a train of 2 red and 7 blue cubes. Turn it around: now it's 7 + 2. Ask whether the number of cubes changed (no). Practice saying turn-around pairs.

questions.q: If 2 + 7 = 9, what is 7 + 2?
Write the turn-around fact for 6 + 3 = 9.

days.guide: Give a short doubles/near-doubles quiz, then play: roll two dice, say the sum, and record. Ask 'Was that a double or near double?'

questions.q: Roll 5 and 5. Sum?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested) and answers: 1) 1+1=2 2) 2+2=4 3) 3+3=6 4) 4+4=8 5) 5+5=10 6) 2+3=5 7) 3+4=7 8) 4+5=9 9) 1+2=3 10) 5+4=9. Proficient: 9–10 correct and can explain one near double using a double.

weeks.prep: Triangle fact-family cards (draw triangles with the total at top and parts in bottom corners: 3-5-8, 2-7-9, 4-6-10, 1-5-6, 3-4-7), counters, a number line 0–10.
misconceptions: Writing 5 − 8 = 3 in a fact family: the biggest number (the whole) always comes first in a subtraction fact.
Thinking subtraction is unrelated to addition: use 'think addition' language ('4 and what make 9?').
For ? − 2 = 6, subtracting 2 from 6: remind that the unknown is the start — act it out: 'Something, take away 2, leaves 6' so the start is 8.

days.guide: Write 9 − 4. Make a 9-cube train, break off 4, and ask '4 plus what makes 9?' Count the rest: 5. Say 'Subtraction is finding a missing part.'
Show a triangle card 3-5-8. Write the four facts together: 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8, 8 − 3 = 5, 8 − 5 = 3. Have your child do the 2-7-9 card alone.

questions.q: Write the fact family for 2, 7, 9.
Which number is the whole in 3, 5, 8?

days.guide: For 8 − ? = 5, start at 8 on the number line and count jumps back to 5 (3 jumps). For ? − 2 = 6, start at 6 and jump forward 2 to find the start (8).
Cover one corner of a triangle card with your thumb and have your child name the hidden number and say a fact that proves it. Switch roles.

questions.q: Card shows 10 on top, 4 at the bottom, one corner hidden. What is hidden?
Card shows 3 and 4 at the bottom, top hidden.

days.guide: Your child writes fact families for 5 triangle cards, then solves missing-number equations.

questions.q: Fact family for 1, 5, 6.

weeks.prep: Fact flash cards within 10, 2 dice, the free Math Learning Center 'Number Rack' app (apps.mathlearningcenter.org), Khan Academy login, and a printed 30-fact sheet for Friday.
misconceptions: Counting on fingers for every fact: name a strategy for each card and practice a few 'just know it' facts each day.
Subtracting the larger number from the smaller after a dice roll: always say 'big number minus small number'.
Rushing on timed checks and guessing: tell your child accuracy comes first; speed grows with practice.

days.guide: Lay out fact cards and four strategy labels: count on, doubles, make 10, think addition. Your child places each card under the strategy they'd use and explains. Accept any sensible choice.

questions.q: Which strategy for 6 + 1?
Which strategy for 8 − 3?

days.guide: Open the Number Rack app. Say a fact (e.g., 6 + 3) and have your child slide beads to show it in one push (5 red + 1 white on the top row, then 3). Ask how they see the total without counting by ones.

questions.q: Show 7 on the rack in one push. What did you move?
Show 4 + 4. Total?

days.guide: Roll two dice. Your child adds them, then subtracts the smaller from the larger, recording both: e.g., 5 and 3 → 5 + 3 = 8 and 5 − 3 = 2. Do 10 rounds.

questions.q: Roll 6 and 2: sum and difference?
Roll 4 and 4.

days.guide: Sit with your child for 15–20 minutes of Khan Academy 'add and subtract within 10.' Watch for slow facts and jot them down for flash-card review.
Give the 30-fact sheet with a 2-minute timer (record how many are correct), then a short written test. Practice missed facts next week in games.

weeks.assessment_key: Fluency goal: 30 facts correct in 2 minutes (proficient); 20–29 developing; under 20 keep practicing with games. Written test (suggested): 1) 5+4=9 2) 10−3=7 3) 6+2=8 4) 8−8=0 5) 3+3=6 6) 9−4=5 7) Fact family 2,6,8: 2+6=8, 6+2=8, 8−2=6, 8−6=2 8) 7+?=10 → 3 9) Story: 9 kites, 2 fly away → 7 10) Story: 4 red and 5 blue → 9.

weeks.prep: A pan balance or coat-hanger balance (hang two cups from a hanger with string), 20 identical cubes or coins, and a 10-item true/false sheet (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking '=' means 'the answer comes next' (so 6 = 6 or 5 + 2 = 2 + 5 look 'wrong'): always read = as 'is the same as' and test with the balance.
Solving 3 + 4 = ? + 5 as 7 (writing the sum in the box): model that both sides must balance — 7 on the left, so the right must also be 7: ? = 2.
Calling 7 = 8 − 1 false because the answer is on the left: check by computing each side.

days.guide: Put 4 cubes and 2 cubes in one cup and 6 cubes in the other. Watch the hanger balance. Say 'Four plus two is the same as six,' and write 4 + 2 = 6 and 6 = 4 + 2.

questions.q: Is 6 = 4 + 2 true?
Left cup has 3 + 3, right cup has 5. Does it balance?
questions.a: No: 6 is not the same as 5.

days.guide: Write the four equations one at a time. For each, your child builds both sides with cubes and decides true or false: 6 = 6 (true), 7 = 8 − 1 (true), 5 + 2 = 2 + 5 (true), 4 + 1 = 5 + 2 (false: 5 vs 7).

questions.q: Is 4 + 1 = 5 + 2 true?
Is 7 = 8 − 1 true?

days.guide: Write 3 + 4 = ? + 5. Put 3 + 4 cubes on the left side (7). Put 5 on the right and ask how many more to balance (2).
Your child writes 3 true and 2 false equations on cards and gives them to a family member to sort. They must check the family member's answers with cubes.

questions.q: Is 9 = 9 true?
Make 2 + 3 = 1 + ? true.

days.guide: Give the 10-item true/false quiz. Your child may use cubes and should circle T or F.

questions.q: Is 8 = 4 + 4 true?
Is 3 + 2 = 6 true?

weeks.prep: Counters, story mats (draw a pond, fishbowl, and balloon bunch on paper), and 6 story cards with unknowns in different places (see key).
misconceptions: Adding the two numbers in 'start unknown' stories (? + 3 = 8 answered as 11): act it out — hide the starting amount and add 3 to see the total must be 8.
Thinking a story with 'more came' always means add the numbers given: ask 'What do we already know — the start, the change, or the total?'
Writing equations that don't match the story: read the story slowly and write a box for the number you don't know.

days.guide: Read 'There were 5 ducks. Some more came. Now there are 9.' Put 5 counters on the pond mat and add counters one at a time until there are 9, counting the added ones (4). Write 5 + ? = 9, ? = 4.

questions.q: There were 6 bees. Some more came. Now there are 10. How many came?

days.guide: Read 'Some fish were in a bowl. 3 more were added. Now there are 8.' Use a cup to 'hide' the unknown start. Work backward: take away the 3 added to find the start: 5.

questions.q: Some kids were at the park. 2 more came. Now there are 7. How many were there first?

days.guide: Read '10 balloons, some popped, 6 left.' Your child draws 10 balloons and crosses out balloons until 6 are left, then counts the crossed-out ones (4). Write 10 − ? = 6.

questions.q: 9 cookies, some were eaten, 5 are left. How many were eaten?

days.guide: Help your child invent a story for 7 − ? = 4 (e.g., '7 cars, some drove away, 4 are left'). They illustrate it and solve: 3.

questions.q: Tell a story for ? − 2 = 5 and solve.
questions.a: Example: Some birds, 2 flew away, 5 left; there were 7.

days.guide: Read 6 problems aloud; your child uses counters or drawings and writes an equation with a box for each unknown.

questions.q: 8 frogs; some hopped away; 3 left. How many hopped?
Some cards; I got 4 more; now 9. How many first?

weeks.assessment_key: Six problems (suggested) and answers: 1) 4 + ? = 7 → 3 2) ? + 5 = 9 → 4 3) 8 − ? = 2 → 6 4) ? − 3 = 6 → 9 5) 6 + 4 = ? → 10 6) 9 − 5 = ? → 4. Proficient: 5–6 correct with a matching equation; developing: 3–4; beginning: 0–2 (reteach start-unknown with cups).

weeks.prep: Connecting cubes in 2 colors, 3 dice, paper for drawing models, and a printed Unit 3 test (see key).
misconceptions: In 'Mia has 3 more than Leo (4)', answering 3: build Leo's train, then Mia's is the same plus 3 more: 7.
In 'Leo has 2 fewer than Mia (9)', adding to get 11: 'fewer' means Leo's train is shorter — 9 − 2 = 7.
Adding three numbers in a fixed left-to-right order only: encourage looking for a 10 or a double first.

days.guide: Build Leo's 4-cube train. Build Mia's train to match Leo's, then add 3 more cubes in another color. Count Mia's: 7. Write 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.q: Leo has 4 shells. Mia has 3 more than Leo. How many does Mia have?
Kai has 5 cars. Lily has 4 more than Kai. How many does Lily have?

days.guide: Build Mia's 9-cube train. Make Leo's train 2 shorter by lining up and removing 2. Count: 7. Write 9 − 2 = 7.

questions.q: Mia has 9 rocks; Leo has 2 fewer. How many does Leo have?
A red ribbon is 8 inches; a blue ribbon is 3 inches shorter. How long is the blue one?

days.guide: Roll 3 dice. Before adding, your child looks for two numbers that make 10 or a double and adds those first, then adds the third. Record each equation.

questions.q: Roll 4, 6, 3. Sum?
Roll 5, 2, 5.

days.guide: Read mixed problems one at a time. Before writing an equation, your child draws a model (cube train or picture). Ask: what do we know, what are we finding?

questions.q: Tom has 6 apples. He has 2 more than Ann. How many does Ann have?
3 red, 4 blue, and 2 yellow balls. How many?

days.guide: Give the unit test, reading every item aloud; allow cubes.

questions.q: Is 5 + 3 = 4 + 4 true?
Nina has 8 stickers, Joe has 5. How many more does Nina have?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test (suggested): 1) 6 + ? = 9 → 3 2) ? − 4 = 5 → 9 3) Leo has 5, Mia has 2 more → 7 4) Mia has 8, Leo has 3 fewer → 5 5) 2 + 5 + 3 → 10 6) T/F 7 = 3 + 4 → T 7) T/F 6 + 1 = 5 + 3 → F 8) 4 + 5 = ? + 6 → 3 9) Jen has 10 beads, Al has 7; how many fewer does Al have → 3 10) 10 − ? = 2 → 8. Proficient 9–10; developing 6–8.

weeks.prep: Two ten-frames side by side (double ten-frame), 20 counters in two colors, a deck of cards (Ace–9), and 10 make-ten problems (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking 13 is '1 and 3' rather than 10 and 3: show the full ten-frame plus 3 every time you say a teen number.
When making ten for 9 + 4, forgetting to take the 1 from the 4 (answering 14): physically move one counter and see 10 + 3.
Making ten from the smaller number instead of the bigger: start with the number closest to 10.

days.guide: Show 13 as a full ten-frame and 3 in the second frame. Say 'Thirteen is ten and three: 10 + 3 = 13.' Your child builds 11–19 the same way and writes each as 10 + __.

questions.q: Show 16 on the double ten-frame. Write it as 10 + ?
What is 10 + 9?

days.guide: Put 9 in one frame and 4 in the other. Move 1 counter from the 4 to fill the 9-frame. Now there is 10 + 3 = 13. Have your child explain 'I moved 1 to make 10.'
For 8 + 5, put 8 in the first frame. It needs 2 to make 10, so split 5 into 2 and 3. 10 + 3 = 13. Record the thinking as a number bond under the 5.
'Make Ten and Go': flip two cards; add them by making ten, saying each step aloud ('9 needs 1, so 7 becomes 1 and 6; 10 + 6 = 16'). The correct sum earns the cards.

questions.q: Flip 7 and 5. Explain.
Flip 9 and 8.

days.guide: Your child solves 10 make-ten problems, drawing the ten-frames for each.

weeks.assessment_key: Answers: 1) 9+2=11 2) 9+3=12 3) 9+5=14 4) 9+7=16 5) 8+3=11 6) 8+4=12 7) 8+6=14 8) 7+4=11 9) 7+5=12 10) 6+5=11. Drawing should show the bigger number's frame filled to 10 and the leftover ones. Proficient: 9–10 correct with drawings that show the make-ten step.

weeks.prep: Dominoes, 2–3 dice, counters, 2 egg cartons, two ten-frames, and a doubles quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking 7 + 8 = 7 + 7 = 14 (forgetting the 'plus one'): say 'double the smaller one, then add 1 more.'
Believing changing the order of three addends changes the sum: rearrange cubes and recount to prove the total stays the same.
Mixing up 6+6=12 and 7+7=14: link to real things — egg carton rows (6+6=12), two weeks (7+7=14).

days.guide: Fill 6 cups on each side of an egg carton: 6 + 6 = 12. Build 7+7 through 10+10 on double ten-frames and list them: 12, 14, 16, 18, 20. Chant the list.
Solve 7 + 8 aloud: 'I know 7 + 7 = 14. 8 is one more, so 15.' Play a card game: flip two cards that are one apart and solve as near doubles.
Read 'Sam saw 4 birds, 6 squirrels, and 3 rabbits.' Ask which two to add first; 4 + 6 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13. Write 4 + 6 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: How many animals did Sam see?

days.guide: Build 5 + 2 + 5 with cube trains, then rearrange to 5 + 5 + 2. Both are 12. Explain that adding the 5s first makes a 10, which is easier.

questions.q: Why is 5 + 2 + 5 = 5 + 5 + 2 true?
questions.a: Same numbers in a different order; both equal 12.

days.guide: Give the doubles quiz and 3 three-addend word problems; read each aloud.

questions.q: Lia has 3 red, 3 blue, and 4 green beads. How many?

weeks.assessment_key: Doubles quiz (suggested): 6+6=12, 7+7=14, 8+8=16, 9+9=18, 10+10=20, 6+7=13, 7+8=15, 8+9=17. Word problems: 1) 5 apples, 4 pears, 5 plums → 14 2) 3 + 8 + 7 stickers → 18 3) 2 + 6 + 4 kids → 12. Proficient: 10–11 of 11 correct and shows grouping (making 10 or a double) in at least one word problem.

weeks.prep: Two ten-frames, counters, a 0–20 number line, and 5 subtraction story cards (see day 4).
misconceptions: Taking 4 from 13 by removing ones from the full ten-frame first, then getting confused: take the 3 loose ones first to get to 10, then 1 more.
For 'think addition' (15 − 7), answering 22 by adding: say '7 plus what makes 15?'
Counting the starting number as a jump on the number line: always 'land then count' jumps.

days.guide: Show 13 (full ten-frame + 3). For 13 − 4, take away the 3 extra counters first (to 10), then 1 more from the ten-frame: 9. Write 13 − 3 − 1 = 9.
For 15 − 7, ask '7 plus what makes 15?' Count up from 7 to 10 (3) and 10 to 15 (5): 3 + 5 = 8. Practice with 3 more.
For 16 − 9, start at 16 on the number line and jump back 6 to 10, then 3 more to 7. Or jump forward from 9 to 16 (7 jumps). Compare both ways.
Read 5 subtraction stories aloud. Your child chooses a model (ten-frame, number line, or drawing) and writes an equation.

questions.q: Ben had 14 cars and gave away 5. How many are left?
There are 18 kids; 9 are boys. How many girls?
11 grapes, ate 3. How many left?

days.guide: Give a short strategy quiz. Then ask your child to explain 14 − 6 aloud using any strategy.

questions.q: Explain 14 − 6.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) 13−4=9 2) 15−6=9 3) 12−7=5 4) 16−8=8 5) 11−2=9 6) 17−9=8 7) 14−5=9 8) 18−9=9. Explanation rubric for 14 − 6 = 8: 4 = names a strategy and shows each step (take to ten or think addition); 3 = correct answer, partial explanation; 2 = counts back by ones only; 1 = incorrect.

weeks.prep: Counters, number line 0–20, Khan Academy login, paper for illustrated problems, and a Unit 4 test (see key).
misconceptions: Using key words only ('more' = add) without understanding: always ask the child to retell the story and show it with a model.
Listing only a few ways to make 15: be systematic — 15 + 0, 14 + 1, 13 + 2 ... 8 + 7.
Writing story problems that have no question: remind that a story problem ends with 'How many...?'

days.guide: Present one of each problem type (add to, take from, put together, compare) within 20. For each, your child models with counters before writing an equation.

questions.q: 12 birds; 5 fly away. How many left?
Ana has 13 beads, Joe has 9. How many more does Ana have?
8 red and 7 blue blocks. How many blocks?

days.guide: Ask 'How many ways can you make 15 by adding two numbers?' Your child lists them in order and explains the pattern to a family member.

questions.q: List the ways to make 15 with two numbers 0–15.
If one part is 6, what is the other?

days.guide: Sit with your child for a Khan Academy 'add and subtract within 20' set. Note missed facts and practice them with cards afterward.
Your child writes and illustrates two story problems (one adding, one subtracting) for a family member to solve, and writes the answer key on the back.

questions.q: Check: 'I had 15 crayons. I lost 6. How many now?'
What must every story problem have at the end?

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test, reading story problems aloud.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 4 test (suggested): Facts: 9+4=13, 8+7=15, 6+6=12, 7+5=12, 15−8=7, 13−6=7, 16−7=9, 11−4=7. Stories: 1) 9 cats, 8 dogs → 17 2) 14 apples, 6 eaten → 8 3) Al has 12, Bo has 7, how many more does Al have → 5 4) 4 + 5 + 6 pencils → 15. Proficient 11–12 of 12; developing 8–10.

weeks.prep: A bag of mixed buttons (or LEGO, toy cars), chart paper, crayons, and a simple pre-made picture graph for Friday (see key).
misconceptions: Making tally marks as 5 straight lines instead of 4 with a slash: model 'four standing, the fifth lies across.'
Drawing picture-graph pictures different sizes so rows look unequal: use one sticker or same-size square per vote, lined up.
Answering 'how many more' by giving one category's total: compare the two rows and count the extras.

days.guide: Dump a bag of buttons and ask 'How could we sort these?' Sort by color first and label each group. Then mix and sort again by number of holes (2 or 4). Discuss that the same things can be sorted different ways.

questions.q: What did we sort by first? Second?
Name one category you made.
questions.a: Example: red buttons / buttons with 2 holes.

days.guide: Make a 3-row chart with category names. Your child records each sorted button with a tally mark, bundling fives. Then count each row.

questions.q: Show 7 with tally marks.
questions.a: One bundle of 5 (4 lines with a slash) and 2 more lines.

questions.q: A row has 2 bundles of 5 and 1 more. How many?

days.guide: Survey family about favorite fruit (apple, banana, orange). Your child draws one fruit picture per vote in rows, same size and lined up, and adds a title.

questions.q: Why should each picture be the same size?
questions.a: So you can compare rows fairly; one picture = one vote.

questions.q: What does a graph need besides pictures?
questions.a: A title and labels for each category.

days.guide: Look at the fruit graph and have your child ask and answer questions: How many in all? Which is most? How many more chose apples than bananas?

questions.q: Apples 6, bananas 3, oranges 4. How many people in all?
How many more chose apples than bananas?

days.guide: Give a pre-made picture graph (e.g., Pets: dogs 7, cats 5, fish 2) and ask 5 questions.

questions.q: Which pet is least popular?
How many more dogs than cats?

weeks.assessment_key: Graph (suggested): Favorite Pets — dog 7, cat 5, fish 2. Questions & answers: 1) How many chose dog? 7 2) Which is most popular? dog 3) How many in all? 14 4) How many more chose dog than fish? 5 5) How many fewer chose cat than dog? 2. Proficient 5/5; 4 = developing.

weeks.prep: Clipboard, tally sheet with 3 categories, 1-inch grid paper, crayons, and a 3-category bar graph for the data quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Starting bars above the baseline or skipping squares: each bar starts at the bottom line, one square per vote.
Forgetting labels or a title: check 'Could someone else tell what this graph is about?'
Thinking 'how many more' is found by adding: compare bar heights and count up from the shorter bar.

days.guide: Help your child pick a survey question with exactly 3 answer choices (e.g., favorite pet: dog, cat, fish). Write the question and choices on a tally sheet.

questions.q: Why only 3 choices?
questions.a: So answers are easy to sort and graph; everyone must pick one of the three.

questions.q: Is 'What's your name?' a good survey question?
questions.a: No — everyone has a different answer, so it can't be sorted into a few categories.

days.guide: Your child asks at least 10 people (phone or in person) and makes a tally for each answer. Count each row at the end.

questions.q: If you surveyed 10 people and dog got 5 and cat got 3, how many chose fish?
How do you show a tally of 6?
questions.a: A bundle of 5 and 1 more line.

days.guide: On grid paper, draw a baseline, label the 3 categories underneath, and color one square up for each tally. Add a title and number labels on the side.

questions.q: Dog had 5 tallies. How tall is its bar?
What goes at the top of the graph?

days.guide: Your child writes 3 statements ('More people like dogs than fish') and 2 how-many-more questions, with answers.

questions.q: Dog 5, cat 3, fish 2: how many more chose dog than cat?
Write a true statement about this data.
questions.a: Example: Dog is the favorite; fish got the fewest votes.

days.guide: Your child presents the graph to family. Then give the data quiz on a 3-category bar graph.

questions.q: Bars: red 4, blue 8, green 6. Which is most?
How many more chose blue than red?

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric: 4 = question with 3 choices, 10+ tallies, bar graph with title, labels, accurate bars, 3 statements and 2 correct how-many-more questions; 3 = one element missing; 2 = graph inaccurate or missing several parts; 1 = incomplete. Data quiz graph (suggested Favorite Colors: red 4, blue 8, green 6): 1) blue most 2) red fewest 3) total 18 4) blue − red = 4 more 5) green − red = 2 more.

weeks.prep: A 120 chart (print one), dry-erase sleeve and marker, scissors to cut chart puzzle pieces, and a cup of 50–120 pieces of dry pasta.
misconceptions: Saying 'one hundred ten, one hundred eleven' after 109 incorrectly (e.g., 'two hundred'): practice 100–120 reading the chart: 'one hundred one... one hundred nine, one hundred ten.'
Writing 1001 for one hundred one: show that 101 has 3 digits: 1 hundred, 0 tens, 1 one.
Confusing teen and -ty numbers (14 vs 40): emphasize the ending: four-TEEN vs FOR-ty.

days.guide: Point to 47 and count aloud by ones to 120 together, pointing to each square. Pay special attention to crossing decades (59→60, 99→100, 109→110).

questions.q: What comes after 89? After 109?
Count from 97 to 103.

days.guide: Color the 5 column (5, 15, 25...) and the 30 row. Ask: going down a column, what changes? (tens digit goes up 1). Across a row? (ones digit goes up 1).

questions.q: What is just below 34 on the chart?
What pattern do numbers in the 7 column share?

days.guide: Cut a chart into small puzzle pieces with only one number showing. Your child fills in the missing numbers using the left/right = 1, up/down = 10 rules.

questions.q: A piece shows 56. What is right of it? Below it?
What number is above 72?

days.guide: Your child counts a pile of 50–120 pasta pieces by making groups of 10, then counts by tens and ones (e.g., 8 tens and 3 → 83).

questions.q: 9 groups of ten and 4 extra. How many?
11 groups of ten and 2 extra.

days.guide: Your child writes numbers from a starting point (e.g., from 88 to 120) and fills in 3 chart pieces.

questions.q: Write the numbers from 98 to 104.
What comes between 114 and 116?

weeks.assessment_key: Counting check: counts aloud from 47 to 120 with correct decade changes. Chart puzzle (suggested pieces): center 45 → left 44, right 46, above 35, below 55; center 78 → 77, 79, 68, 88; center 103 → 102, 104, 93, 113. Writing: from 88 to 120 every number in order with no reversals. Proficient: all decade transitions correct and 11–12 of 12 puzzle cells correct.

weeks.prep: About 100 craft sticks, rubber bands, base-ten blocks or paper strips (ten-strips and single squares), a place-value mat (two columns: Tens | Ones), and a list of 10 numbers for the quiz.
misconceptions: Reading 34 as 3 and 4 (not 30 and 4): always say '3 tens is 30.'
Thinking 1 ten and 15 ones is not 25: count it out — 10 + 15 = 25; trade 10 ones for a ten to show 2 tens 5 ones.
Writing 504 for 'five tens and four ones': have the child build it and write the tens digit then the ones digit.

days.guide: Your child counts out sticks, bundling every 10 with a rubber band. Count bundles by tens and then loose sticks by ones: '10, 20, 30, 31, 32.'

questions.q: 3 bundles and 2 loose sticks. How many?
How many sticks in 5 bundles?

days.guide: Lay out 1 bundle and say 'one ten is 10.' Keep adding bundles: 2 tens = 20 ... 9 tens = 90. Write each on the mat.

questions.q: How many tens is 60?
What number is 8 tens?

days.guide: Build 34 with 3 rods and 4 units on the mat, writing '3 tens 4 ones = 34.' Your child builds 58 and 71 the same way.

questions.q: How many tens and ones in 58?
Build 71. How many rods and cubes?

days.guide: Build 25 as 2 rods and 5 units. Trade one rod for 10 units: now 1 ten 15 ones. Count to show it's still 25.

questions.q: Is 1 ten 15 ones the same as 25?
Show 43 another way.

days.guide: Give 10 numbers; your child builds each on the mat and writes tens and ones.

questions.q: 67 = __ tens __ ones
4 tens 0 ones = ?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 23 = 2t 3o; 45 = 4t 5o; 60 = 6t 0o; 18 = 1t 8o; 92 = 9t 2o; 37 = 3t 7o; 81 = 8t 1o; 50 = 5t 0o; 74 = 7t 4o; 99 = 9t 9o. Proficient 9–10 built and recorded correctly.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, index cards for a match game (e.g., 47 / 40 + 7 / 4 tens 7 ones), mystery-number riddle cards, and pictures of blocks for day 4.
misconceptions: Saying 'eleven is one and one': build 11 as a ten and one.
Writing expanded form as 4 + 7 instead of 40 + 7: point to the tens digit and ask 'What is it worth?'
Writing 'sixty-three' as 603: build 6 tens 3 ones and write 63.

days.guide: Build 11–19 one at a time with a ten rod and ones. Your child says 'Fourteen is one ten and four ones' for each.

questions.q: 17 = 1 ten and __ ones
What is 1 ten and 2 ones?

days.guide: Show 47 with blocks and write 47 = 40 + 7. Play a matching game pairing standard form, expanded form, and tens/ones cards.

questions.q: Write 63 in expanded form.

days.guide: Read riddles aloud: 'I have 6 tens and 3 ones. What am I?' Let your child build and answer, then make riddles for you.

questions.q: 6 tens and 3 ones?
I have 2 ones and 9 tens.
I have 1 ten and 0 ones.

days.guide: Say numbers in words ('fifty-eight') and show pictures of blocks; your child writes the numeral.

questions.q: Write 'seventy-one'.
Picture: 4 rods, 6 cubes.

days.guide: Give a place-value quiz with teen and two-digit numbers.

questions.q: Write 16 in expanded form.
How many tens in 90?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) 13 = 1 ten 3 ones 2) 19 = 10 + 9 3) 52 = 50 + 2 4) 7 tens 8 ones = 78 5) 30 + 4 = 34 6) 'eighty-six' = 86 7) 'forty' = 40 8) riddle 5 tens 1 one = 51 9) blocks 2 rods 9 cubes = 29 10) 1 ten 1 one = 11. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, symbol cards (>, <, =), a deck of cards 0–9 (Ace = 1, paper 0s), and the 12-item comparison quiz.
misconceptions: Comparing ones first (thinking 38 > 42 because 8 > 2): always compare tens first.
Reversing < and >: 'the open mouth eats the bigger number' or 'the small point points to the smaller number.'
Reading 52 < 61 backward: read left to right: '52 is less than 61.'

days.guide: Build 42 and 38 with blocks. Compare the rods first: 4 tens vs 3 tens, so 42 is greater even though 8 ones > 2 ones.

questions.q: Which is greater: 42 or 38? Why?
Which is less: 56 or 59?

days.guide: Teach the symbols: > means greater than, < means less than, = means equal. Your child writes comparisons for 10 pairs and reads each aloud.
Each player flips 2 cards and makes a 2-digit number. Compare and record with a symbol (e.g., 73 > 46). Bigger number wins the round.

questions.q: You make 35, I make 53. Record it.
With cards 6 and 2, what is the biggest number you can make?

days.guide: Your child orders 5 two-digit numbers from least to greatest by sorting tens first, then ones.
Give the 12-item comparison quiz.

weeks.prep: 120 chart, base-ten blocks, a list of 20 numbers for mental 10 more/10 less, plus-shaped chart pieces, and a Unit 6 test (see key).
misconceptions: Thinking 10 more than 47 is 48 (adding 1): show on the chart that 10 more is straight down, not to the right.
Changing the ones digit when finding 10 less: only the tens digit changes; the ones stay the same.
Forgetting that 10 more than 95 is 105 (not 96 or 15): count it on the 120 chart.

days.guide: Put a finger on 34. Move down one row: 44 (10 more). Move up: 24 (10 less). Practice with 6 numbers.

questions.q: 10 more than 34?
10 less than 71?

days.guide: Build 56 with blocks. Add a ten rod: 66. Remove a rod: 46. Ask which digit changed.

questions.q: 10 more than 56?
questions.a: 66 — the tens digit changes from 5 to 6.

questions.q: 10 less than 20?

days.guide: Say 20 numbers quickly and your child says 10 more or 10 less without the chart. If stuck, picture the blocks.

questions.q: 10 more than 89?
10 less than 15?
10 more than 105?

days.guide: Give plus-shaped pieces with only the center filled. Your child fills up (10 less), down (10 more), left (1 less), right (1 more).

questions.q: Center 67: fill up, down, left, right.
Center 100?

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test, reading aloud as needed.

questions.q: What is 7 tens 2 ones?
10 less than 43?

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks (at least 10 rods and 20 units), a hundred or 120 chart, and a quiz of 10 addition problems (see key).
misconceptions: Adding the ones digit of 30 + 20 as '5' or writing 32: 3 tens + 2 tens = 5 tens = 50.
Adding tens to ones (34 + 20 = 36): line up tens with tens and ones with ones.
In 38 + 6, writing 314 (3 tens and 14 ones written side by side): trade 10 ones for a ten: 4 tens 4 ones = 44.

days.guide: Show 30 + 20 with 3 rods and 2 rods: 5 rods = 50. Say 'three tens plus two tens is five tens.' Practice 40 + 50, 10 + 60.
Build 34 and add 2 rods: 54. Then show on the chart: start at 34 and move down 2 rows.
Build 42, add 5 units: 4 tens 7 ones = 47. No new ten needed because 2 + 5 is less than 10.
Build 38 + 6. 8 ones + 6 ones = 14 ones, so trade 10 ones for a rod. Or think: 38 + 2 = 40, then 40 + 4 = 44.
Your child solves mixed problems by drawing tens as sticks and ones as dots.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, paper for open number lines, and a strategy quiz (see key).
misconceptions: Jumping by ones on an open number line for +30: show one big jump of 10 three times (47 → 57 → 67 → 77).
Drawing ten-sticks and dots but miscounting the new ten: circle 10 dots and turn them into a stick.
Writing an explanation that only restates the answer ('it is 63'): prompt with 'First I…, then I…'.

days.guide: Draw an open number line. For 47 + 30, mark 47 and draw three jumps of 10: 57, 67, 77. For 56 + 8, jump 4 to 60 then 4 more to 64.
Use quick drawings: a line for a ten, a dot for a one. 25 + 7: 2 sticks 5 dots + 7 dots = 12 dots, circle 10 to make a stick: 3 sticks 2 dots = 32.
Read problems like 'A farm has 46 chickens and 8 ducks. How many birds?' Your child chooses a strategy and writes an equation.

questions.q: 46 chickens and 8 ducks. How many birds?
A farm has 35 cows; 40 more come. How many cows?

days.guide: Your child solves 59 + 4 and writes one sentence telling how: e.g., 'I added 1 to make 60 and then 3 more to get 63.'

questions.q: Write a sentence for 28 + 5.
questions.a: 33; e.g., 'I added 2 to get 30, then 3 more is 33.'

days.guide: Give the strategy quiz; each problem needs an answer and a drawing or sentence.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested): 1) 36+40=76 2) 58+7=65 3) 44+5=49 4) 27+60=87 5) 69+3=72 6) 15+9=24. Explanation rubric: 4 = correct answer plus clear steps (make a ten, jumps, or tens/ones); 3 = correct with partial explanation; 2 = some errors but sensible strategy; 1 = no strategy shown.

weeks.prep: Ten rods, a 120 chart, 10 real dimes (or paper), and a quiz of 10 subtracting-tens problems.
misconceptions: Subtracting 3 from 70 when asked 70 − 30 (getting 67): say 'seven tens take away three tens.'
Moving down the chart instead of up to subtract tens: up = 10 less.
Thinking dimes are worth 1 each: a dime is 10¢, so count dimes by tens.

days.guide: Lay out 7 rods (70). Take away 3 rods. Count: 4 rods = 40. Write 70 − 30 = 40.
For 90 − 60, ask '60 plus what makes 90?' Count up by tens: 70, 80, 90 = 3 tens = 30.
On the chart, start at 80 and jump up 3 rows to subtract 30: 70, 60, 50.
Count 8 dimes: 10, 20 ... 80¢. Take away 5 dimes: 30¢ left. Write 80¢ − 50¢ = 30¢.

questions.q: You have 6 dimes and spend 4. How much is left?

days.guide: Your child solves 10 subtracting-tens problems with rods or the chart.

weeks.prep: Base-ten blocks, open-number-line paper, 120 chart, a die, Khan Academy login, 5 worked problems with errors (see day 4), and the Unit 7 test.
misconceptions: Adding tens and ones together as if both were ones (40 + 3 = 7): build both numbers before adding.
When an error is found, erasing without explaining: ask your child to tell what went wrong.
Racing to 100 by adding without tracking regrouping: keep the running total on blocks.

days.guide: Set up three stations (blocks, number line, 120 chart). Give one problem per station (e.g., 46 + 20, 38 + 5, 70 − 40); your child solves each a different way.
Sit with your child for Khan Academy 'add within 100' and 'subtract tens' practice. Ask them to explain one problem aloud.
Race to 100: roll a die and choose to add that many tens or ones to your total. Record each move as an equation (e.g., 34 + 5 = 39). First to exactly 100 (or closest without going over) wins.

questions.q: You're at 74 and roll 2. If you add tens, where are you? Ones?
You're at 96 and roll 4 ones.

days.guide: Show 5 worked problems with mistakes, e.g., 45 + 30 = 48; 36 + 7 = 313; 80 − 20 = 78; 29 + 4 = 23; 54 + 20 = 56. Your child finds and fixes each and says what went wrong.

questions.a: 43; 13 ones = 1 ten 3 ones, so 4 tens 3 ones.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test.

weeks.prep: Pencils and crayons of different lengths, string or yarn, scissors, 3 ribbons of different lengths, household objects.
misconceptions: Comparing without lining up ends (an object looks longer because it sticks out on one side): always line up the ends on a table edge.
Thinking the string must be the same length as both objects: the string 'stands in' for the first object; cut or mark it, then compare to the second.
Ordering by thickness or size instead of length: point along the long side only.

days.guide: Give 3 pencils or crayons. Line up their bottom ends on the table edge and order shortest to longest. Ask your child to use the words shortest, longer, longest.

questions.q: Which is longest, and how do you know?
questions.a: The one that sticks out farthest when the ends are lined up.

questions.q: If A is longer than B and B is longer than C, which is shortest?

days.guide: Compare pairs of household objects (spoon vs fork, book vs remote) by lining up ends. Your child says '___ is longer than ___.'

questions.q: Why must you line up the ends?
questions.a: So you only compare how far each one reaches; otherwise the comparison isn't fair.

questions.q: Which is longer, a spoon or a crayon (usually)?

days.guide: You can't move the door or table, so stretch string along the table's length and cut/mark it. Hold the string against the door width. Ask which is longer.

questions.q: How does the string help?
questions.a: It copies the table's length so we can compare it with the door.

questions.q: The string is longer than the door's width. What does that mean?
questions.a: The table is longer than the door is wide.

days.guide: Your child finds 3 things longer and 3 shorter than their arm by holding them alongside their arm, and draws them.

questions.q: Name something longer than your arm.
questions.a: Example: a broom, a couch, a bed.

questions.q: Something shorter?

days.guide: Your child orders 3 ribbons and uses a string to compare a couch and a bed, explaining their method.

questions.q: Explain how you compared the couch and the bed.
questions.a: Stretch string along the couch, mark it, then hold it along the bed; whichever is longer than the string is longer.

questions.q: Which ribbon goes first in shortest to longest?

weeks.assessment_key: Performance task rubric: 4 = lines up ends to order 3 ribbons correctly AND uses string to compare couch and bed with a clear explanation ('the string was the couch's length; the bed was longer than the string'); 3 = correct ordering and comparison with prompting; 2 = orders ribbons but cannot do indirect comparison; 1 = does not line up ends.

weeks.prep: A box of same-size paper clips, connecting cubes, a book, spoon, shoe, pictures of measurements with gaps/overlaps (draw 3), and a recording sheet.
misconceptions: Leaving gaps or overlapping units: line units end to end, touching, starting exactly at the edge.
Mixing unit sizes (big and small paper clips): every unit must be the same size.
Thinking a bigger number always means a longer object even with different units: more cubes than clips doesn't mean the object grew — smaller units give bigger counts.

days.guide: Show how to measure a book: start the first clip at the edge, line clips end to end with no gaps, and count. Record each measurement as 'The book is __ paper clips long.'

questions.q: Where must the first paper clip start?
questions.a: Exactly at the end of the object.

questions.q: If 7 clips fit along the spoon, how long is it?

days.guide: Show drawings with gaps between clips, overlapping clips, and one correct. Your child circles the mistakes and explains.

questions.q: Why is a gap a mistake?
questions.a: The gap is part of the length but not counted, so the number is too small.

questions.q: What happens if clips overlap?
questions.a: You count more clips than fit, so the number is too big.

days.guide: Measure the same book, spoon, and shoe with cubes. Compare: 'The book was 6 clips but 9 cubes.' Ask why.

questions.q: Why did the book measure more cubes than clips?
questions.a: Cubes are shorter than paper clips, so it takes more of them.

questions.q: Did the book's length change?

days.guide: Measure the hallway with heel-to-toe steps. Then a family member measures it. Compare the numbers and discuss why they're different.

questions.q: Why did Dad need fewer steps?
questions.a: His feet are longer, so each step covers more distance.

questions.q: How could we get the same number?
questions.a: Use the same unit, like the same paper clips or a ruler.

days.guide: Your child measures 5 objects with clips, records each, and circles any measurement where gaps/overlaps happened.

questions.q: A pencil is 5 clips and a crayon 3 clips. How much longer is the pencil?
What makes a measurement fair?
questions.a: Same-size units, end to end, no gaps or overlaps.

weeks.assessment_key: Recording sheet: answers vary by object; check that each entry has a number and the unit ('6 paper clips'). Proficient (4) = all 5 measured with units touching end to end, starting at the edge, counts within 1 of your own check, and any gap/overlap correctly circled; 3 = one error; 2 = several gaps or no units named; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Connecting cubes, 10 toys of different lengths, grid paper, and a Unit 8 test (see key).
misconceptions: Putting a toy in the wrong category because the boundaries are unclear: decide rules first, e.g., short = 1–4 cubes, medium = 5–8, long = 9 or more.
Graph bars not starting at zero: draw a baseline and color from the bottom.
Answering how-many-more by adding the bars: subtract or count up from the shorter bar.

days.guide: Your child decides 3 length categories and writes cube ranges for each (e.g., short 1–4, medium 5–8, long 9+).

questions.q: Why do we need number rules for each category?
questions.a: So every toy fits in exactly one category.

questions.q: A toy is 6 cubes. With our rules, which category?

days.guide: Your child measures 10 toys with cubes and records each length and category.

questions.q: A toy car is 4 cubes long. Category?
A doll is 10 cubes. Category?

days.guide: Make a bar graph with 3 bars (short, medium, long), one square per toy, with a title and labels.

questions.q: If 4 toys are short, how tall is that bar?
What should the title say?

days.guide: Ask how-many-more questions about the graph.

questions.q: Short 4, medium 4, long 2. How many more short than long?
How many toys in all?

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test.

questions.q: A pencil is 8 cubes, a crayon is 5 cubes. Which is longer, and by how much?
Rope A is longer than rope B; rope B is longer than rope C. Is A longer than C?

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 8 test (suggested): 1) Order 3 pictured strips shortest to longest (check order). 2) A is longer than string; string is longer than B → A is longer than B. 3) Measure a pictured line with paper clips drawn end to end (count shown, e.g., 6). 4) Circle the picture with a gap → the gapped one. 5) Graph short 3, medium 5, long 2: most = medium; how many more medium than long = 3; total = 10. Proficient: all correct or one error.

weeks.prep: Paper plate, brass fastener, construction paper hands (short hour hand, long minute hand), markers, a real analog clock, and 10 clock pictures for Friday.
misconceptions: Mixing up the hour and minute hands: the short hand tells the hour; the long hand tells minutes.
At half past, reading the hour as the next number (2:30 read as 3:30) because the hour hand is near 3: the hour hand is between 2 and 3, so it's still 2-something.
Writing 3:00 as 3:0 or 30:0: show digital clocks — hours, colon, two digits for minutes.

days.guide: Write 1–12 around a paper plate (12, 3, 6, 9 first so spacing is even). Attach a short and a long hand with a fastener. Your child shows 'clock face parts' and names each hand.

questions.q: Which hand is shorter?
What number is at the top of a clock?

days.guide: Show times on the hour: long hand on 12, short hand on the hour. Your child shows and writes 3:00, 7:00, 12:00.

questions.q: The short hand is on 8 and the long hand on 12. What time?
Show 5:00. Where are the hands?
questions.a: Short hand on 5, long hand on 12.

days.guide: Move the long hand to 6 and show that the hour hand slid halfway between two numbers. Read it as 'half past' or ':30'.

questions.q: Long hand on 6, short hand halfway between 4 and 5. Time?
Where is the hour hand at 9:30?

days.guide: Your child draws 4–5 parts of their day (breakfast, lessons, lunch, play, bed) with a clock time for each, on the hour or half hour.

questions.q: If lunch is at 12:30, draw the hands.
questions.a: Long hand on 6, short hand halfway between 12 and 1.

questions.q: Which comes first: 8:00 or 7:30?

days.guide: Your child reads 10 clock pictures and writes each time.

questions.q: Hands: short on 2, long on 12.
Short between 11 and 12, long on 6.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz (suggested 10 clocks): 1:00, 3:00, 6:00, 9:00, 12:00, 2:30, 5:30, 7:30, 10:30, 12:30 — your child should write each as shown. Proficient 9–10; watch especially for half-past times read one hour too late.

weeks.prep: Real pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters; a magnifying glass; a coin chart sheet; play-store toys with price tags under 50¢; a Unit 9 test.
misconceptions: Thinking bigger coins are worth more (nickel more than dime): the dime is smallest but worth 10¢.
Counting all coins by ones: count dimes by tens first, then pennies by ones.
Mixing up penny and nickel names: penny is copper-colored, 1¢; nickel is silver, bigger, 5¢.

days.guide: Let your child examine each coin with a magnifier: color, size, edge (dimes and quarters have ridges), and the pictures. Sort into four piles and name them.

questions.q: Which coin is copper colored?
Which coin is the smallest?

days.guide: Make a coin chart: penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢. Tape or draw each coin next to its value.

questions.q: How much is a nickel worth?
Which is worth more, a dime or a nickel?

days.guide: Lay out 3 dimes and 4 pennies. Count dimes by tens (10, 20, 30) then pennies by ones (31, 32, 33, 34): 34¢. Connect to 3 tens and 4 ones.

questions.q: 4 dimes and 2 pennies?
6 dimes and 0 pennies?

days.guide: Price toys under 50¢ with tags. Your child 'buys' them by counting out dimes and pennies (and nickels if ready).

questions.q: A toy costs 23¢. Which dimes and pennies pay exactly?
You buy a 15¢ toy. Pay with a dime and what?

days.guide: Give the Unit 9 test: read and write 6 clock times, and name and value 8 coins.

questions.q: Name and value of the silver coin with ridges, biggest of the 4.
Short hand between 6 and 7, long hand on 6.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 9 test (suggested): Times: 4:00, 8:00, 11:00, 1:30, 3:30, 9:30. Coins (show real coins): penny 1¢, nickel 5¢, dime 10¢, quarter 25¢, penny 1¢, dime 10¢, nickel 5¢, quarter 25¢. Proficient: 13–14 of 14 correct.

weeks.prep: Cut-out paper shapes (triangles, squares, rectangles, hexagons, circles, trapezoids in different sizes and colors), straws cut into pieces, playdough, and a geoboard or Math Learning Center Geoboard app.
misconceptions: Thinking a 'tipped' triangle or rotated square isn't the same shape: turn the paper shape and recount sides and corners.
Using color or size to name a shape: say 'shape names come from sides and corners, not color or size.'
Thinking a square isn't a rectangle: a square has 4 straight sides and 4 square corners, so it is a special rectangle.

days.guide: Your child sorts shapes into groups by number of sides and corners (3, 4, 6, 0) and names each group.

questions.q: How many sides and corners does a triangle have?
How many does a hexagon have?

days.guide: Show a big red triangle and a small blue triangle. Ask why both are triangles. Guide to 'both have 3 straight sides and 3 corners and are closed.'

questions.q: Are these both triangles: a big red one and a small blue one?
questions.a: Yes — both have 3 straight sides and 3 corners; color and size don't matter.

questions.q: Is a shape with 3 sides but a gap a triangle?

days.guide: Your child builds shapes from straws joined by playdough balls: a triangle, a square, a rectangle, a hexagon. Count straws (sides) and balls (corners).

questions.q: How many straws for a square?
How many playdough balls for a hexagon?

days.guide: Give attribute challenges on the geoboard: 'Make a shape with 4 sides that's not a square,' 'Make a triangle that touches 5 pegs on its sides.'

questions.q: Make a shape with 4 sides and 4 square corners but not all sides equal. What is it?
Make a closed shape with 3 sides.

days.guide: Give the attribute quiz: circle triangles/rectangles in a mixed set and write why color/size do not matter.

questions.q: Why do color and size not matter?
questions.a: Shapes are named by sides and corners; a triangle is a triangle in any color or size.

questions.q: Is a circle a polygon with sides?
questions.a: No — a circle has no straight sides or corners.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz rubric: Circle all triangles (3 sides, 3 corners, closed) and rectangles (4 sides, 4 square corners, including squares) in the set; do not circle open shapes, circles, or shapes with curved sides. Explanation: 'Shapes are named by sides and corners; color and size don't change that.' Proficient: all shapes sorted correctly and explanation names sides/corners.

weeks.prep: Household boxes, cans, balls, a cone (party hat or ice-cream cone), paper and crayons for tracing, pattern blocks (or the free Pattern Shapes app), and a hexagon outline.
misconceptions: Calling a cube a square or a sphere a circle: flat shapes are 2-D; solids you can hold are 3-D.
Thinking a cylinder's face is a rectangle: trace the end of a can — it's a circle.
Thinking there's only one way to fill a hexagon: try 2 trapezoids, 6 triangles, 3 rhombuses, or mixed.

days.guide: Hunt for 3-D shapes at home: cube (dice), cylinder (can), cone (party hat), sphere (ball), rectangular prism (cereal box). Your child labels or draws each.

questions.q: A soup can is what solid shape?
A cereal box?

days.guide: Trace the flat faces of a box, can, and cube on paper. Name the 2-D shape each makes.

questions.q: Trace the end of a can. What shape?
What shape are the faces of a cube?

days.guide: Your child fills a hexagon with pattern blocks: 2 trapezoids, then 6 triangles, then 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles. Count blocks each time.

questions.q: How many triangles make a hexagon?
How many trapezoids make a hexagon?

days.guide: Build a castle from boxes and cans. Your child names each solid used (cylinder towers, cube blocks, cone roofs).

questions.q: What solid makes a good tower that can roll on its side?
Which solid has no flat faces?

days.guide: Your child fills a hexagon outline three ways, records each by drawing or tracing, and names 5 solid shapes.

questions.q: Name 3 ways to fill a hexagon.
questions.a: 2 trapezoids; 6 triangles; 3 rhombuses (or 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles; 2 rhombuses + 2 triangles).

questions.q: Name 5 solid shapes.
questions.a: Cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, rectangular prism.

weeks.assessment_key: Composition task: any 3 different correct fillings, e.g., (a) 2 trapezoids, (b) 6 triangles, (c) 3 rhombuses, (d) 1 trapezoid + 3 triangles, (e) 2 rhombuses + 2 triangles, (f) 1 trapezoid + 1 rhombus + 1 triangle. Solids: cube, cylinder, cone, sphere, rectangular prism. Proficient: 3 correct fillings recorded and all 5 solids named.

weeks.prep: Paper circles and rectangles to fold, scissors, crayons, a tortilla or sandwich, pictures of shapes cut into equal and unequal parts, and a Unit 10 test (see key).
misconceptions: Calling any 2 pieces 'halves': halves must be the same size.
Thinking more pieces means bigger pieces (fourths are bigger than halves): compare by laying a fourth on top of a half.
Thinking a 'fourth' and a 'quarter' are different: they're two names for the same thing.

days.guide: Fold a paper rectangle and circle in half. Unfold and check if the two parts match by folding again. Color one half.

questions.q: How many halves make a whole?
What makes them halves?
questions.a: The two parts are equal in size.

days.guide: Fold a rectangle and circle in half and in half again to get 4 equal parts. Label each part 'one fourth' or 'one quarter.'

questions.q: How many fourths make a whole?
What's another name for a fourth?

days.guide: Show pictures of shapes cut into parts. Your child sorts into 'equal shares' and 'not equal shares' and explains.

questions.q: A circle is cut into 2 different-sized pieces. Are they halves?
questions.a: No — the pieces must be equal.

questions.q: A rectangle is cut into 4 equal strips. What is each called?

days.guide: Cut a tortilla in halves, then another in fourths. Compare: which piece is bigger, a half or a fourth? Then enjoy the snack.

questions.q: Which is bigger: one half or one fourth of the same tortilla?
If you share a sandwich equally with 3 friends (4 people), what does each person get?

days.guide: Give the Unit 10 test.

questions.q: How many sides does a trapezoid have?
Draw a line to cut a circle into halves.
questions.a: A line straight through the center.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 10 test (suggested): 1) Triangle: 3 sides, 3 corners 2) Rectangle: 4 sides, 4 square corners 3) Circle the rectangles (including a square) 4) Pattern blocks to make a hexagon: e.g., 2 trapezoids 5) Name the solid: can = cylinder, ball = sphere 6) Shade one half of a rectangle 7) Shade one fourth of a circle 8) Which picture shows equal shares? 9) Which is bigger, a half or a fourth of the same pizza? half 10) How many quarters in a whole? 4. Proficient 9–10.

weeks.prep: Flash cards within 20, base-ten blocks, symbol cards, 6 story problems (see day 3), favorite games (cards, dice), and a 20-item cumulative review.
misconceptions: Forgetting earlier strategies (make ten, doubles) under pressure: post a strategy reminder chart.
Mixing up 10 more and 1 more on place value problems: build with blocks to check.
Reading compare stories as add problems: ask 'Are we finding a total or a difference?'

days.guide: Give the final within-10 fluency check (30 facts in 2 minutes) and practice within 20 with flash cards. Note which strategies your child uses.
Your child builds 5 two-digit numbers, finds 10 more/10 less for each, and compares pairs with >, <, =.

questions.q: Build 48. 10 more? 10 less?
Compare 48 and 84.

days.guide: Your child solves 6 mixed story problems and writes an equation for each: add to, take from, compare, three addends.

questions.q: Mia had 12 shells and found 5 more. How many?
Raj has 15 cards; Sam has 9. How many more does Raj have?

days.guide: Play favorite math games from the year (Make Ten Go Fish, War, Race to 100). Ask your child to say each fact aloud.

questions.q: In Go Fish for 10, you hold a 4. What do you ask for?
Roll 6 and 6. Double?

days.guide: Give the 20-item cumulative review part 1.

questions.q: Is 9 + 3 = 6 + 6 true?
What is 7 tens 5 ones?

weeks.prep: Printed end-of-year assessment part 2 (see key), a math journal or folded paper booklet, a clipboard for the scavenger hunt, and favorite game materials.
misconceptions: Rushing through a long test: break it into short sessions and read aloud.
Forgetting half-hour clock reading: review the hour hand 'between two numbers' before the test.
Confusing nickel and dime values: review the coin chart.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year assessment part 2 over 1–2 sittings, reading every item aloud.

questions.q: Short hand between 3 and 4, long hand on 6. Time?

days.guide: Your child makes a journal page about a favorite thing they learned, with a drawing and an example problem they solved.

questions.q: What was your favorite math topic? Show one example.
questions.a: Answers vary; the example must be correct (e.g., 9 + 4 = 13 by making ten).

questions.q: What strategy helps you add 9 + 6?

days.guide: Take a walk outside to find shapes (circles, rectangles), numbers (house numbers, signs), and things to compare by length. Record findings on a clipboard.

questions.q: Find a rectangle outside. How do you know?
questions.a: Example: a door — 4 sides, 4 square corners.

questions.q: Read a house number. How many tens and ones?

days.guide: Your child teaches a family member a favorite game and explains the math in it ('In Go Fish for 10, you need partners that make 10').

questions.q: What math do you practice in Make Ten Go Fish?
What does War practice?
questions.a: Comparing numbers and how many more.

days.guide: Hold a math fair: your child shows projects (survey graph, clock, journals) and explains one thing they learned.

questions.q: Tell how your survey graph works.
questions.a: Each square/bar shows how many people chose that answer; the tallest bar is the most popular.

questions.q: What's one thing you got better at?

weeks.assessment_key: End-of-year part 2 (suggested) with answers: 1) 30+40=70 2) 52+7=59 3) 38+5=43 4) 61+20=81 5) 90−40=50 6) Order 3 pictured objects by length (check) 7) A shoe measured with cubes drawn → count shown 8) Clocks: 7:00, 10:30, 2:30 9) 3 dimes 4 pennies = 34¢ 10) Name & value: quarter 25¢, nickel 5¢ 11) Graph (apples 5, pears 2, grapes 4): most = apples, total 11, apples − pears = 3 12) Circle the shape with 3 sides & 3 corners (triangle) 13) Shade one fourth of a square. Proficient: 90% or better; review any weak strand over the summer.
